lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Princeton, New Jersey. April, nineteen fifty-five. An old man in a hospital bed asks for only one thing.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: My papers, please. And my glasses. I am not finished.

lines.speaker: DOC
lines.text: Professor Einstein, you need to rest.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Rest? I have rested enough. There is still one equation missing.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: That's him. And you've known him for fifty years. To see how, we go back to a newspaper ad.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Bern, Switzerland. Nineteen-oh-two. You're a broke young student, and a tiny ad catches your eye.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Private lessons in mathematics and physics. Trial lesson free. Albert Einstein. Free? I'll take it.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: A young man with wild dark hair opens the door. He's twenty-three, and he has no job.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Come in, come in! You want to learn physics? Good. Then tell me first: what is time?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Time? It's, um, what clocks measure?

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Ha! And what do clocks measure? Time! You see? We are already in trouble.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: So what is time, really?

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: I don't know yet. That is the fun part!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The trial lesson lasts four hours. He never asks you for a single franc.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Forget the lessons. Come back tomorrow. Talking is better than teaching.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Soon you're part of a tiny club with his friends, Maurice Solovine and Conrad Habicht. They give it a grand name.

lines.speaker: HAB
lines.text: I hereby open the session of the Olympia Academy! Tonight's feast: one sausage, some cheese, and tea.

lines.speaker: SOL
lines.text: And tonight's book is David Hume. Albert, you start.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Hume says we never see a cause. We see one thing, and then another. So, can we be sure of anything?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: We can be sure the sausage is gone.

lines.speaker: HAB
lines.text: Psst. For his birthday, we bought real caviar. Watch this.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: He's busy explaining Galileo's law of inertia. He eats the whole plate, and never notices.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: So that was caviar? Well. Fine food is wasted on a peasant like me.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: He needs money, so a friend helps him get a job: Technical Expert, Third Class, at the Swiss Patent Office. Soon after, he marries Mileva Marić, a physics student from his university.

lines.speaker: MIL
lines.text: Albert, you'll be reading patents for electric clocks all day.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Exactly, Mileva! Clocks! How do you make two clocks in two cities agree? That is a deep question.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Nineteen-oh-five. A warm evening in May. He drags you and his best friend, Michele Besso, to a café.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Besso, you must help me. I think I am going mad.

lines.speaker: BES
lines.text: Calm down, Albert. Which problem is it this time?

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Light! If I chase a beam of light, does it slow down for me? It cannot. Light always moves at the same speed.

lines.speaker: BES
lines.text: Then something else must give way.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: But what? Space? Time?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The next morning, at the patent office, he walks straight up to Besso. No hello.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Thank you. I've completely solved the problem.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Time is not the same for everyone. Two clocks, moving differently, do not agree.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: So my now and your now aren't the same?

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Not if we are moving. Isn't it wonderful?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Albert, how many papers did you send out this year?

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Five! Light, atoms, relativity, and my doctorate. Not bad for a clerk, no?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: That year, a twenty-six-year-old patent clerk publishes papers on light, on atoms, and on relativity. They call it his miracle year.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: You wrote one more paper? It's only three pages!

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Short, but important. Mass and energy are the same thing, in different clothes.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: So how much energy is in, say, one raisin?

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Take its mass. Multiply by the speed of light, squared. A very, very big number.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: E equals m c squared. One gram of matter holds the energy of about twenty thousand tons of explosives. In nineteen-oh-five, nobody imagines where this leads.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Nineteen-oh-seven. He's still at the patent office, staring out of the window.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Ach! I just had the happiest thought of my life.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: They finally promoted you?

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Better! A man falling from a roof does not feel his own weight.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Until he hits the ground.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Before that! Falling and floating are the same. So gravity is not a pull at all. It is space and time, bending.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Turning that one thought into mathematics takes him years. By nineteen twelve, he begs an old classmate for help.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Grossmann, you must help me, or I'll go crazy!

lines.speaker: GRO
lines.text: Riemann's geometry? Albert, it's a terrible mess. Physicists should stay away from it.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Then I will make a mess, my friend.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: November, nineteen fifteen. Berlin. He tests his finished theory on an old puzzle: the strange orbit of Mercury.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: It fits. Exactly! My heart is racing. I am beside myself with joy!

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: But the real test needs the Sun. If I'm right, starlight bends around it. We can only see that during a total eclipse.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: May, nineteen nineteen. The British astronomer Arthur Eddington photographs the eclipse from an island off Africa.

lines.speaker: EDD
lines.text: The stars have shifted. Just as Einstein predicted.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Professor, they confirmed it! But what if the photos had proved you wrong?

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Then I would have felt sorry for the dear Lord. The theory is correct.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Overnight, he's the most famous scientist on Earth. Newspapers call it a revolution in science.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: And now the Nobel Prize! For relativity, right?

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: No! For my little paper on light, from nineteen-oh-five. They still don't trust relativity.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Brussels, nineteen twenty-seven. The greatest physicists alive meet to argue about the strange rules of atoms.

lines.speaker: BOHR
lines.text: At the smallest scales, nature is a game of chance. We can only know probabilities.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: I cannot believe that. God does not play dice.

lines.speaker: BOHR
lines.text: Einstein, stop telling God what to do!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: At every meeting, he brings a new thought experiment to break the theory. And every time, Bohr finds an answer.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Bohr! A box full of light, with a clock inside. Weigh the box, and your uncertainty is broken!

lines.speaker: BOHR
lines.text: Ah, but a clock that moves in gravity runs differently, Albert. Your own relativity saves me!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: So who's winning?

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Bohr, today. Tomorrow? We shall see.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Experiments mostly side with Bohr. But Einstein's objections lead to quantum entanglement, the idea behind today's quantum computers.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Nineteen thirty-three. Hitler takes power. Einstein is visiting America, and he never goes back.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: I will not live in a country where people are not equal before the law.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The Nazis seize his home and burn his books. He settles in Princeton. Six years later, a visitor brings a warning.

lines.speaker: SZI
lines.text: German scientists have split the uranium atom. A chain reaction could make a bomb of enormous power.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: I never even thought of that.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: What will you do?

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: Then we must warn the President. Before Hitler gets there first.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: His letter to Roosevelt helps start the atomic bomb project. Einstein never works on it himself.

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: I made one great mistake in my life, when I signed that letter. But there was the danger that the Germans would make it first.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Back to that hospital bed. April eighteenth, nineteen fifty-five. He dies in his sleep, at seventy-six. His last calculations lie beside him.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: He never found the equation he was looking for.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: But the GPS in your phone corrects for relativity every day. Without it, your position would drift by about ten kilometers a day.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Lasers, solar panels, even the first photo of a black hole, all trace back to his ideas.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Professor, what should I tell my own students one day?

lines.speaker: EIN
lines.text: The important thing is not to stop questioning. I have no special talents. I am only passionately curious.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: So, if you were his student, which question would you chase for fifty years? Tell me in the comments.
